extracted.intended_audience: students, scientists, and philosophers studying induction and the logic of causal inference
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and tests for deciding whether an observed uniformity is a law of causation or an empirical (derivative) law, and for distinguishing lawful connexion from chance through experimental design, frequency comparison, and averaging. Includes criteria for elimination of chance and basic foundations of probability calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical law status when supported only by Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: No generalization amounts to more than an empirical law when the only proof on which it rests is that of the Method of Agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Method of Agreement can ascertain the whole of the circumstances common to all cases in which a phenomenon is produced, but it cannot determine which common circumstance is the cause; therefore conclusions from it alone should be treated as empirical (derivative) laws until confirmed by the Method of Difference or explained deductively (accounted for a priori).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on extending empirical laws beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws can only be received as true within the limits of time and place (and circumstance) in which they have been found true by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because empirical laws may depend on unknown 'collocations' of causes, we cannot safely extend them beyond the bounds of actual experience without trial or further explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign 1 that a law of causation is derivative: evidence of intermediate links
rubrics_metrics.description: If between antecedent a and consequent b there is evidence of some intermediate link (x), then the law 'a causes b' is resolvable into at least two laws and is derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chemical synthesis (production of water involves unseen corpuscular steps); processes of vegetative life are corpuscular and thus the higher-level laws are derivative. The presence or surmise of intermediate phenomena indicates the law is not ultimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sign 2 that a law is derivative: extremely complex antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent is an extremely complex phenomenon, its effects are probably compounded from the effects of its different elements, so the observed uniformity is likely derivative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: weight (sum of minute particles' weights) and meteorological sequences (column of air plus vapor). Complex antecedents usually decompose into simpler causes; ultimate laws tend to be simpler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish derivative empirical laws from ultimate laws by demand for deductive explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Both kinds of empirical laws (those known to be laws of causation but presumed resolvable, and those not known to be laws of causation) demand being explained by deduction and serve as tests for deductive results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until explained and connected with ultimate laws, such uniformities have not attained the highest degree of certainty and are less general and certain than the simpler laws from which they may result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of causes limits Method of Agreement — need for multiplicity of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The Method of Agreement cannot prove causation because a phenomenon may have many causes; coinciding antecedents may be accidental overlap of different true causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As the number of instances pointing to the same antecedent increases, uncertainty diminishes; but the number and kind of instances necessary to reach practical certainty must be judged case-by-case by comparing observed coincidence frequency against what chance would produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of chance as coincident conjunction without grounds for uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: An event occurring by chance is better described as a coincidence from which we have no ground to infer a uniformity: two or more phenomena conjoined in no way related through causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurrent coincidence alone does not suffice to prove law; what matters is whether coincidence occurs more often than chance (properly defined accounting for base frequencies) would account for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-rate adjustment: deduct expected coincidence from observed to detect law
rubrics_metrics.description: To infer a causal connection from frequency of co-occurrence, deduct from the observed frequency that amount which would be expected from the absolute frequencies of the phenomena themselves if they were independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if A occurs in 1/2 of cases and B in 1/3, expected co-occurrence by chance is 1/6. Any excess above that residual supports some connection; any deficit suggests repugnance/negative connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative-proportion test for connexion
rubrics_metrics.description: If A occurs in a larger proportion of the cases where B is than of the cases where B is not, and equivalently B occurs in a larger proportion of the cases where A is than where A is not, then there is some connection through causation between A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a generalization of subtracting chance: compare conditional proportions rather than absolute counts to detect association indicative of common or causal causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null example caution: ubiquitous antecedents produce worthless coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: If A exists always (ubiquitous antecedent), its co-existence with B, however constant, proves nothing about causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: fixed stars co-exist with all observed phenomena but are not their cause. Always-accounting antecedents create expected co-occurrence equal to their ubiquity and must be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of causes and need for Elimination of Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: When a constant cause A's effect is blended with many variable causes, we must ascertain the effect of the variable causes taken together by making many trials preserving A invariable and taking the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If repeated trials (varied across circumstances) yield results that oscillate about a stable mean, that mean is the effect attributable to A; the oscillation is the effect of chance (variable causes). The test of sufficiency is when further trials do not materially change the mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of residual constant causes by averaging (detecting small effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect is chiefly produced by changeable causes but contains a small constant component, repeated trials and averaging may reveal a non-zero mean indicating a constant cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: detecting loaded dice by large number of throws yielding a persistent bias; diurnal barometer variation discovered by comparing average barometer heights at different hours. Conclusion valid when increasing trial number stabilizes the average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for assessing whether frequency exceeds what chance accounts for
rubrics_metrics.description: The question of whether a given frequency of coincidence is more than chance can account for has no general numeric answer; the proper determination depends on estimating how often chance alone would produce the coincidence within the same limits of space and time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reasoning about base frequencies and expected co-occurrence; examine whether observed excess (or deficit) remains after accounting for varying prevalence and other causal/repugnant factors. Use mathematical theory of probability where appropriate for limits and variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplacean reduction for calculating chances (equally possible cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability can be measured by reducing events to a number of equally possible cases and taking the ratio of favorable cases to all possible cases, but this requires that we know one of the events must happen and have no reason to prefer one over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laplace's formal criterion requires equally undecided cases; critics note that empirical evidence of equal frequency is also required in practice — theoretical symmetry alone may be insufficient without observed frequency supporting equality.
